story.title: The backlash about data centers might really just be about electricity

facts.text: But spending a few days in Data Center Alley left me wondering if it’s really the proxy that Lehane describes.
I came away convinced that the data center backlash is more about electricity than Big Tech admits.
The industry can improve its image, but it can’t escape the physical consequences of its enormous appetite for electricity.
The overwhelming majority of AI data centers being built elsewhere in the country are not designed this way.
The scale desired is so massive that companies are setting up in rural areas where there is virtually no grid infrastructure to connect to.
Building there means bringing your own power (so-called “behind the meter” power), in the form of natural-gas-powered turbines.
Companies also build diesel generators for backup.
Anthropic, for example, has reportedly agreed to pay $3.4 billion for gas turbines in what’s described as the largest power generation purchase by an AI company.
Even if grids were nearby, they’d be unlikely to serve the amount of power demanded.
The smallest data centers attractive for AI training are 300 megawatts.
The notion of data center companies’ bringing their own power might seem attractive at first, because they wouldn’t be straining the grid.

But generating electricity at this scale inevitably affects surrounding communities, and when public utilities build infrastructure of this magnitude, communities have traditionally expected a say in where it goes.
Now, private companies are undertaking projects on a similar scale.
Companies might also try their chances abroad; Google, in fact, announced the day after the elections that it will spend $15 billion on data center projects in Malaysia.
The average data center operating in this part of Virginia today has a power capacity of 54 megawatts.
That’s more than the power draw of the Denver International Airport .
But the real fault line is electricity: drawing it from the grid and generating it onsite provoke different kinds of backlash, neither easily solved by public relations.
The backlash to data centers isn’t really about water or electricity.
Greg Abbott has moved from cutting ribbons for big data center projects to issuing a list of demands about their power usage, location and economic contributions .
Economic analyst James Pethokoukis has calculated that even if water consumption by data centers quadruples in 2030, they’ll still take just 1% of our supply.
Enforce transparency about power and water usage .
Governments are already requiring the industry to generate its own electricity, and policymakers are even pushing data centers to provide a net increase in power.
• Email letters@star-telegram.com (preferred).
Opinion articles provide independent perspectives on key community issues, separate from our newsroom reporting.
Research indicates that data centers can actually help cut electricity prices because higher demand means more production.
We love to hear from Texans with opinions on the news — and to publish those views in the Opinion section.
That would save far more water than shutting down every data center.

In response to my post about this data center backlash outside of Kansas City (specifically Independence, Missouri), I’ve been fielding the range of ideas people have about hyperscale AI data centers.
More than 160 new AI data centers have popped up across the U.S. in the past three years—a 70% increase from the last three year period, according to a Bloomberg News analysis .
In many instances, they’ve landed in communities with high competition for scarce water resources.
A mid-sized data center consumes as much water as a small town , while larger ones require up to 5 million gallons of water every day—as much as a city of 50,000 people.
They also consume massive amounts of electricity.
On July 18, a national day of protest against data centers saw 142 protests across 42 states.
